definition: A person who has sexually or morally deviated from accepted norms; the dominant Catholic-influenced term used to condemn non-normative sexuality, especially homosexuality.
notes: Core term of mid-20th-century Catholic and state-medical discourse condemning homosexuality in Brazil; persists in conservative religious and family contexts; 'desviado do caminho de Deus' (deviated from God's path) is a common phrasing.

definition: A morally corrupt or sexually deviant person; implies near-satanic corruption of divinely ordained natural order in Catholic theological framing.
notes: Functions as both adjective and noun; the theological sense of corruption of natural law is more salient in Brazilian use than in secular English; commonly applied to paedophiles, gay men, and kink practitioners in conservative discourse.

definition: Morally transgressive, especially in sexual conduct; used in Catholic-influenced Brazilian discourse to condemn any sexuality outside marriage or Church teaching.
notes: Applied broadly in conservative Brazilian contexts to homosexuality, premarital sex, divorce, and contraception; near-universal recognition across generations; frequently deployed in political speech against LGBTQ+ rights.

definition: Sexually or socially offensive behavior that violates public decency norms; used in both religious and legal registers in Brazil.
notes: Appears in Brazilian Penal Code provisions on obscenity and indecency (art. 233); also ubiquitous in everyday Catholic-influenced moral speech about dress, language, or public conduct.

definition: Sexually explicit or grossly offensive material or behavior lacking redeeming value; used in both legal and moral-religious discourse.
notes: Standard orthography is 'obsceno'; 'obceno' is a common popular variant reflecting phonological simplification. Used in Brazilian criminal law (Código Penal art. 234) and everyday moral condemnation alike.

definition: Lacking decorum and sexual or social propriety; a more formal and elevated synonym of indecente, typically applied to public conduct or dress that shocks bourgeois sensibility.
notes: Higher register than indecente; more common in written or institutional contexts; recognition has declined somewhat among younger speakers who prefer more colloquial terms; carries class inflection beyond purely religious condemnation.

definition: Treating the sacred with irreverence; in sexual contexts, engaging in carnal acts that desecrate the God-given body or violate religious sanctity.
notes: In Brazilian Catholic framing, sexuality outside marriage is profano because it desecrates the body as temple of the Holy Spirit; the sacred/secular binary carries more active doctrinal weight in Brazilian use than in secular English; the English 'profane' has weakened considerably in everyday usage.

definition: A distinct Brazilian gender identity of feminine-presenting individuals assigned male at birth who typically maintain their male genitalia and self-identify within a culturally specific category separate from the Western transgender woman concept.
notes: Not equivalent to transvestite (cross-dresser) or transgender woman; travesti is a recognized sui generis category in Brazilian sociology and trans activism with its own political organizations and community history predating Western transgender discourse in Brazil; the identity carries specific class and racialized dimensions tied to street sex work and carnaval culture.

definition: The practice or clinical condition of cross-dressing; in Brazilian psychiatric and legal usage also loosely applied to the travesti lifestyle and identity.
notes: Clinical borrowing from European psychiatry; largely superseded in community discourse by identity-affirming language; still appears in Brazilian legal and psychiatric documents; conflation with travesti identity is contested and considered reductive by travesti activists.

definition: Highly offensive derogatory slur for a travesti or trans woman; the pejorative augmentative-disparaging suffix -eco intensifies contempt and dehumanization.
notes: The -eco suffix in Brazilian Portuguese commonly marks ugliness, contempt, or poor quality (livreco = bad book); strongly rejected by travesti and trans communities; widely used in hostile street speech, police violence contexts, and hate crimes targeting travestis.

definition: In Brazilian travesti and drag culture, the state of being fully assembled in feminine presentation — makeup, wig, clothing, and accessories all in place; from montar (to assemble or mount).
notes: No direct English equivalent; in drag contexts approximates 'in full drag' or 'serving full beat,' but montada in travesti discourse also describes everyday feminine identity presentation rather than theatrical performance exclusively; the antonym is desmontada (disassembled, out of femme presentation).

definition: A performer who transforms between gender presentations on stage; a broadly neutral term for drag and gender-transformation artists that predates drag queen as the dominant label in Brazil.
notes: Older and more neutral than drag queen; covers theatrical transformistas who may or may not identify as trans or gay; usage has declined among younger audiences in favor of the English loanword drag queen; historically tied to boate (nightclub) culture in Brazilian cities.

definition: English loanword fully integrated into Brazilian Portuguese; a person who performs exaggerated femininity through elaborate makeup, wigs, costumes, and live entertainment.
notes: Used without phonological modification in Brazilian speech; popularized through RuPaul's Drag Race (widely watched with Portuguese subtitles) and homegrown Brazilian drag competitions; near-universal recognition across age groups post-2015.

definition: English loanword; a person, typically a woman or non-binary person, who performs exaggerated masculinity through costume, prosthetic facial hair, and performance art.
notes: Significantly less well-known in Brazil than drag queen; recognition concentrated among LGBTQ+-adjacent audiences; gaining visibility through queer festivals and feminist spaces but not yet mainstream.

definition: An older clinical and community term for a person whose gender identity differs from their assigned sex at birth, especially one who has undergone or seeks medical transition.
notes: Gradually replaced in community discourse by trans or transgênero; carries medicalization and surgery-oriented implications absent from the broader term trans; still common in Brazilian legal documents, SUS (public health system) protocols, and older journalism.

definition: Short and widely preferred community self-identifier for transgender and gender-nonconforming people; used as both adjective and noun.
notes: The dominant neutral term in Brazilian trans activist communities; used across all registers from casual speech to academic discourse; preferred over transsexual by most community members under 40.

definition: Gender transition; the social, medical, and legal process by which a trans or travesti person aligns their presentation and body with their gender identity.
notes: Maps to the process rather than the identity; closest registry concept (transgender) denotes identity rather than transition process; typically phrased as transição de gênero for precision; used in SUS protocols and trans rights legislation.

definition: To gender-transition; the verbal form, encompassing hormone therapy, social transition, name and pronoun change, and surgical procedures.
notes: Community neologism modeled on English 'to transition'; more common in online forums and activist discourse than in formal writing; maps to the process not the identity; often paired with de gênero.

definition: To undergo hormone replacement therapy as part of gender transition; a Brazilian Portuguese coinage from hormônio (hormone) plus the verb-forming suffix -izar.
english_term: to go on hormones / to start HRT
notes: No English single-word verb equivalent exists; hormonizar condenses a multi-word English phrase into a productive neologism widely used in trans community forums, Tumblr, and Twitter discourse; recognition concentrated in trans and LGBTQ+-adjacent communities.

definition: A trans woman or travesti who has undergone gender confirmation surgery; the feminine past participle of operar used as a community identity marker for surgical status.
notes: Operada vs não-operada is a key social distinction in Brazilian travesti communities; some individuals use operada as a proud identity marker; the term implicitly marks the speaker/referent as feminine through grammatical gender agreement.

definition: A trans woman or travesti who has not undergone gender confirmation surgery; the negated form of operada, used as a stable identity marker rather than necessarily a transitional state.
notes: In Brazilian travesti culture, não-operada is often a permanent identity choice rather than a pre-surgical waiting state; this differs from the Western pre-op framing which implies future surgery is planned; the distinction matters politically for travesti identity advocacy.

definition: The capacity or degree to which a trans person is perceived as their gender identity without being read as transgender; the Brazilian noun form of the concept of passing.
notes: English uses the phrase passing privilege or ability to pass; passabilidade is a single-word Brazilian nominalization common in trans activist and academic discourse that has no direct English noun counterpart; carries strong political valence around safety and social access.

definition: In trans contexts, to be perceived as one's gender identity without being identified as transgender; the Brazilian Portuguese verb for passing as one's gender.
notes: Passar has numerous general meanings (to pass, to go through, to iron clothes); in trans contexts it carries the specific English sense of passing as one's gender and requires disambiguation; typically phrased as passar por mulher or passar por homem.

definition: In LGBTQ+ contexts, to come to recognize and understand one's own sexual orientation or gender identity; the reflexive internal process of sexual and gender self-discovery.
english_term: to come out to oneself / to realize one is queer
notes: Literally to discover oneself; in LGBTQ+ discourse specifically denotes the private internal recognition of queer identity before any disclosure to others, in contrast to assumir-se (the external coming-out act); often used with a temporal marker: se descobriu aos 18 anos.

definition: To come out; to publicly acknowledge or declare one's sexual orientation or gender identity to others; the standard Brazilian Portuguese equivalent of coming out of the closet.
notes: Literally to assume oneself or to own oneself; the dominant phrase in Brazilian LGBTQ+ discourse for disclosing queer identity to family, peers, or publicly; collocates freely: assumir-se gay, assumir-se trans, assumir-se bissexual; near-universal recognition among younger Brazilians.
